::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 13) you can:

1. **explain** why locality limits message passing (oversquashing, the 1-WL ceiling — Week 9's walls) and precisely what full attention changes, at what cost;
2. **define** Laplacian positional encodings and random-walk structural encodings, compute RWSE by hand on small graphs, and explain the eigenvector sign-ambiguity problem and its treatments;
3. **describe** Graphormer's three encodings — centrality, spatial, edge — and how attention *bias* injects structure into a standard transformer;
4. **explain** the GraphGPS recipe (parallel MPNN + attention + PE/SE) and when the hybrid beats either extreme;
5. **choose** between an MPNN and a graph transformer for a stated task and scale, with attention's $O(n^2)$ reality priced in.
:::

## Locality was a choice, not a law

For eight weeks this course has treated one sentence as bedrock: *messages
flow along edges.* Week 9 measured what that sentence costs — signal crushed
290× through a bridge, cycles invisible above the 1-WL ceiling — and Weeks
9–12 sold increasingly clever workarounds: rewiring, structural features,
labeling tricks, a fully-adjacent final layer. Look at that last one again.
The cheapest oversquashing fix of [Alon & Yahav, 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05205)
— *let every node talk to every node, once* — is a single layer of
something you already know intimately
from every other corner of deep learning. This week we stop treating it as
a patch and ask the full question: what happens when the architecture is
**attention all the way down** — every node attending to every node, every
layer, the edge list demoted from law to hint?

Two things happen, and the whole lecture lives in their tension. First, the
walls fall: information travels anywhere in one hop, so oversquashing's
bridges and oversmoothing's depth pressure simply dissolve — the
$O(n^2)$ pairs are all *there*, priced identically. Take one second to
feel how completely: every pathology Weeks 9 and 11 measured — the 290×
bridge crush, the $|\lambda_2|^K$ collapse, the depth-vs-diameter
bookkeeping — was a *consequence of iterated local averaging*, and a
single global layer performs no iteration and respects no locality; the
diseases don't get treated, their preconditions get deleted.

Second — and this is the part naive "graph transformer" attempts learned
painfully — the graph disappears with the diseases. Attention over a
node *set* is permutation-blind in the wrong way: shuffle the atoms of
two different molecules with the same atom counts and pure attention
cannot tell them apart, because nothing in $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top)$
— the stacked query and key matrices, defined properly one section
down — knows an edge from a stranger.

The entire craft of this week is
*re-injecting the graph as features and biases* — and every ingredient
the modern recipes inject is something this course already computed by
hand: random-walk returns (Week 9 cracked CSL with them), Laplacian
eigenvectors (Week 6's frequencies), shortest-path distances (Week 2).
The graph transformer literature is, to a first approximation, this
course's toolbox being fed to a transformer — which is also why this
week, the second-to-last lecture of new machinery, reads like a
reunion: the payoff of teaching fundamentals over frameworks is that
the newest architecture in the field is assembled entirely from parts
you already own.

The collision was inevitable and dated. By 2020, transformers had annexed
language and were annexing vision, and a widely-circulated observation
pointed out what Week 7's template makes obvious: **a transformer *is* a
message-passing network — on the complete graph.** Set the template's
neighborhood to "everyone," the message to a value vector, the aggregation
to attention-weighted summation, and the update to the feed-forward block:
self-attention drops out of the MPNN template as the special case
$N(v) = \mathcal V$, the whole vertex set. The two literatures were one
literature with different
sparsity patterns, and everyone knew which direction the prestige was
flowing.

Yet the first serious attempts to run transformers on graph
benchmarks *lost to GCNs* — the "do transformers really perform bad for
graph representation?" of Graphormer's title
([Ying et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05234)) is not
rhetorical; it was the
community's genuine, measured position. The resolution, and this lecture's
plot: attention was never the problem — the missing *graph* was. A
transformer given the edge information as features and biases stopped
losing, and won an OGB large-scale challenge outright in 2021. The rest of
the field followed within eighteen months.

### One screen of attention, from zero

Because this course assumed no NLP prerequisite, here is the mechanism
itself, small enough to hold.

::: {#def-w13-attention .definition name="Self-attention (query, key, value)"}
Each node $v$ manufactures three vectors from its features by learned
linear maps — a **query** ("what am I looking for"), a **key** ("what
do I offer"), and a **value** ("what do I actually send") — scores
every node's key against its own query, and receives the
softmax-weighted average of the values. Read it as a *soft dictionary
lookup*: the query is the search term, the keys are the index, the
values are the payload.
:::

The whole machine, in one display:

$$
q_v = W_Q h_v, \quad k_v = W_K h_v, \quad \mathbf{v}_v = W_V h_v;
\qquad
\alpha_{vu} = \operatorname{softmax}_u\!\Big(\tfrac{q_v^\top k_u}{\sqrt d}\Big),
\qquad
h_v^{\text{out}} = \textstyle\sum_{u} \alpha_{vu}\, \mathbf{v}_u,
$$ {#eq-w13-attn}

where — $h_v$ is node $v$'s current feature vector; $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ are
the three learned projection matrices; $q_v$ and $k_v$ are $v$'s query
and key; $\mathbf{v}_v$ is its **value vector**, set in bold to keep it
apart from the node name $v$ and the vertex set $\mathcal V$; $d$ is
the key dimension, and dividing by $\sqrt d$ stops dot products from
growing with width; $\operatorname{softmax}_u$ turns the scores over
all nodes $u$ into positive weights $\alpha_{vu}$ summing to one, and
$h_v^{\text{out}}$ is the weight-averaged value $v$ receives.

Feel @eq-w13-attn on three nodes: if $v$'s query matches the first
key strongly and the others not at all — logits $[2, 0, 0]$ — the
softmax hands out weights $[e^2, 1, 1]/(e^2{+}2) \approx
[0.787, 0.107, 0.107]$: mostly
fetching the match but hedging. And if the query matches nothing —
logits $[0, 0, 0]$ — the weights are exactly $[\tfrac13, \tfrac13,
\tfrac13]$: **attention with nothing to say degenerates to
mean-pooling**, a fact that looks like trivia now and becomes a theorem
about the 1-WL ceiling later this lecture.

Multi-head attention runs $H$
of these machines in parallel on split dimensions and concatenates —
$H$ independent listening policies per layer, which is the slot where
Graphormer will later install $H$ independent *distance* policies.

Hold the transformer-is-an-MPNN identity formally for a moment,
because it sharpens everything after. In Week 7 notation, one attention
layer is

$$
h'_v = \operatorname{UPDATE}\!\Big(h_v,\ \sum_{u \in \mathcal V}
\alpha_{vu}\, \operatorname{MSG}(h_u)\Big),
\qquad
\alpha_{vu} = \operatorname{softmax}_u\!\big(q_v^\top k_u / \sqrt d\big),
$$ {#eq-w13-mpnn-attn}

where — $h'_v$ is the post-update representation; $\mathcal V$ is the
whole vertex set (every node is a neighbor); $\operatorname{MSG}$ and
$\operatorname{UPDATE}$ are the Week 7 template's message and update
functions; and the attention weights $\alpha_{vu}$ of @eq-w13-attn play
the adjacency's role — message passing where the
"adjacency" $\alpha$ is *dense, learned, and input-dependent*. Three
consequences fall out. The receptive field is everything at depth 1
(range solved). The cost is the dense matrix: $n^2$ scores per layer per
head (Week 11's bill returns with an exponent). And nothing constrains
$\alpha$ toward the actual edges — the model must *discover* structure
that the MPNN got for free, or be told it. Discovering it from scratch is
wasteful and, on small data, often simply fails; telling it is the craft:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w13-attention.html >}}

{{< include ../assets/d3/w13-attn.html >}}

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** We trained three models on ZINC molecular
property regression at an identical 100-epoch budget: a plain 4-layer MPNN;
the same MPNN with 16-dimensional random-walk encodings added to its
inputs; and a GPS-style hybrid running MPNN and global attention in
parallel. Predict the ordering of their test errors — and which of the two
upgrades costs more compute.

::: {.predict-answer}
Measured: MPNN **0.349** → +RWSE **0.296** → GPS-lite **0.303** (MAE, lower
is better). The structural encoding bought 0.053 for *six extra seconds*;
the attention block bought *nothing over RWSE* while tripling the time —
because ZINC molecules average 23 atoms and four local layers already reach
everything: range was not the bottleneck, expressiveness was, and the
encoding is what treats that. The tuned literature does get GPS to ≈0.070
at ~10× the schedule — both facts are true, and holding them together is
this week's version of the course's oldest lesson.
:::
:::

## The graph, re-entering as position

A transformer needs to be told where its tokens *are* — in text, positions
1, 2, 3; on a graph, there is no such order, and "where" must mean
*structure*. Two families dominate.

**Random-walk structural encodings (RWSE).**

::: {#def-w13-rwse .definition name="Random-walk structural encoding"}
The RWSE of a node is its vector of random-walk *return probabilities*
at every length up to a budget $K$:

$$
\operatorname{RWSE}(v) = \big[(M^1)_{vv},\ (M^2)_{vv},\ \dots,\
(M^K)_{vv}\big], \qquad M = D^{-1}A,
$$ {#eq-w13-rwse}

where — $A$ is the adjacency matrix; $D$ the diagonal degree matrix, so
$M$ is the row-normalized adjacency (Week 2's random-walk operator) and
$(M^k)_{vv}$, the $v$-th diagonal entry of its $k$-th power, is the
probability that a $k$-step walk from $v$ ends back at $v$. Read each
entry as a local structure detector: it is positive exactly when
$k$-step closed walks exist at $v$.
:::

The vector is computed once, offline (Week 11's precompute discipline),
then added to node features through a small linear map. The encoding
entered the transformer diet through the LSPE line of
[Dwivedi et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07875) and is the
default structural diet in GPS
([Rampášek et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12454));
@alg-w13-rwse below is, symbol for symbol, the `rwse_diag` you implement
in Lab 13.

::: {#alg-w13-rwse .algorithm name="RWSE Precompute"}
Computes every node's $k$-step return probabilities by repeated sparse
multiplication with the row-normalized adjacency.

**Input:** adjacency $A$ ($n \times n$); walk length $K$.
**Output:** $R \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times K}$ with $R_{vk} = (M^k)_{vv}$.

1. $d_v \leftarrow \max\big(\sum_u A_{vu},\, 1\big)$ for every node $v$
2. $M \leftarrow \operatorname{diag}(d)^{-1} A$  (row-normalize)
3. $P \leftarrow I$
4. **for** $k = 1 \dots K$ **do**
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$P \leftarrow P M$
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$R_{\cdot k} \leftarrow \operatorname{diag}(P)$  (each node's $k$-step return)
7. **end for**
8. **return** $R$
:::

Two remarks on the listing. The degree clip in step 1 exists for
isolated nodes (divide by one, not zero), and each power in step 5 is a
sparse multiply — $O(KE)$ overall at graph scale, run once and cached
forever; the result enters the model as $x_v \mathrel{+}= W_{\text{rw}}
R_v$, a learned linear map into feature space. And step 6 is where the
teeth are: $R_{v3} > 0$ exactly when $v$ sits on a triangle — the entry
that cracks CSL below. You have computed these numbers before; now
compute them *as a hand exercise*
on the triangle-with-tail, because the numbers teach the concept better
than the definition does:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w13-rwse.html >}}

Walk one entry to own it. The hub (node 2, degree 3) at $k{=}2$: each
neighbor holds probability $\tfrac13$; the two triangle neighbors return
with probability $\tfrac12$ each, the tail with probability 1 — total

$$
\tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac12 \;+\; \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac12 \;+\;
\tfrac13 \cdot 1 \;=\; \tfrac23.
$$

And the $k{=}3$ column is the star: $\tfrac16$ for every
triangle node (walk your triangle around, either direction:
$\tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac12$), and **exactly zero**
for the tail — a 3-step return needs a 3-cycle, and node 3 has none. The
$k{=}3$ return probability *is a triangle detector*, the $k{=}4$ a
4-cycle-and-backtrack accountant, and the whole vector a structural
fingerprint that Week 9's theorems said message passing cannot compute
about itself. That is the entire pitch: the encoding hands the model
answers to questions the architecture provably cannot ask.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w13-rwse.html >}}

Complete the hand table with the tail's $k{=}4$ entry, because it teaches
the accounting style: a 4-step return from node 3 must go out to the hub
and come back twice-removed — $3 \to 2 \to x \to 2 \to 3$ for
$x \in \{0, 1, 3\}$ — with probability

$$
1 \cdot \Big[\tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac12 +
\tfrac13 \cdot 1\Big] \cdot \tfrac13
\;=\; \tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac13 \;=\; \tfrac29 \;\approx\; 0.222:
$$

the hub's own
2-step return rate, rented. Every entry of every RWSE vector decomposes
into such stories, which is why the encoding is *interpretable* in a way
learned embeddings never are — and why Lab 13's asserts can demand your
implementation match to four decimals.

Practicalities, quickly. $K$ (vector length) is a budget knob — 16 to 32
in practice; entries beyond the graph's mixing time flatten toward the
stationary distribution and stop informing (Week 2's convergence,
setting a feature dimension). The whole family generalizes: replace
$M^k$'s diagonal with heat-kernel diagonals or personalized-PageRank
columns and you get sibling encodings with different locality profiles —
the "small zoo of diffusions" from Week 11's SIGN, feeding a transformer
instead of an MLP. And the compute is a Week 11 story: sparse
matrix powers, offline, once, cacheable forever.

Before leaving the definition, collect the payment it makes on a debt
this course has carried since Week 9. The CSL graphs — the two circulant
rings, every node degree-4, that message passing *provably* cannot tell
apart, our cleanest exhibit of the 1-WL ceiling — fall to RWSE at
$k{=}3$: one ring's skip pattern closes triangles, so every node has a
positive 3-step return; the other's does not, so every node's is exactly
zero. Two graphs indistinguishable to arbitrary depths of message
passing are separated by the *third entry* of a vector you can compute
by hand.

In Lab 13 you do exactly that, on your own
implementation, and then separate the triangle-with-tail's members from
its tail node with nothing but a threshold on that entry. The week's
pitch in one artifact: the ceiling was never about how much computation
the network does; it was about which quantities the computation can
express, and the encoding simply hands the unreachable ones in through
the front door.

**Laplacian positional encodings (LapPE).**

::: {#def-w13-lappe .definition name="Laplacian positional encoding"}
Take the graph Laplacian's first $k$ nontrivial eigenvectors — Week 6's
low-frequency modes — and give each node its coordinates in that basis.
Because an eigenvector is defined only up to **sign** (and, within
degenerate eigenspaces, up to rotation), the encoding is well-defined
only modulo those symmetries — the ambiguity every LapPE user must
treat. Read it as a soft global coordinate system:
"where am I on the graph's large-scale shape," complementary to RWSE's
"what does my local structure look like."
:::

You have seen these coordinates
*work* already without the name: the Fiedler vector that split the karate
club in Week 2 assigns every node a signed scalar whose sign is the
faction and whose magnitude is depth-within-faction — one LapPE
dimension, and already a useful position. Stack the next few eigenvectors
and nodes acquire addresses on the graph's principal shapes, the discrete
cousin of sinusoidal positions on a sequence (which are, exactly, the
Laplacian eigenvectors of a path graph — the connection that motivated
LapPE in the first place).

That parenthesis rewards thirty seconds of hand computation, because it
turns "positional encoding" from a metaphor into an identity. The
4-node path's Laplacian eigenvectors are sampled cosines,

$$
v_k(j) = \cos\!\big(k\pi\,(j + \tfrac12)/4\big),
$$ {#eq-w13-lappe}

where — $k$ indexes the eigenvector (the frequency), $j \in \{0, 1, 2,
3\}$ indexes position along the path, and $v_k(j)$ is node $j$'s
coordinate in eigenvector $k$. The first
nontrivial one reads $(0.924,\; 0.383,\; -0.383,\; -0.924)$ down the
path — strictly monotone, a *coordinate along the graph*, with the sign
change marking the midpoint exactly as the karate Fiedler vector's sign
marked the faction line. The transformer literature's sinusoidal
position vectors for sequences are this same object at more frequencies;
LapPE is not "inspired by" transformer positions — on a path graph it
*is* them, and on a general graph it is what they become when the
domain stops being a line. That is why the analogy runs so deep, and
why the same failure (what happens off the training distribution of
positions) recurs in both literatures.

The wrinkle you met in Week 6 bites harder here: an eigenvector is
defined only up to **sign** — $v$ and $-v$ are the same eigenvector — and
within a *degenerate* eigenspace (repeated eigenvalues, guaranteed by any
symmetry in the graph) only up to rotation, so the same graph can hand
the model different encodings on different days, and a test graph's
encoding can be systematically flipped relative to everything seen in
training.

Treatments, in ascending sophistication and cost: randomize
signs during training (augmentation teaches the invariance, spends
capacity), take absolute values (cheap, invariant, lossy — genuinely
different positions collapse), or use architectures invariant by
construction (the SignNet line of
[Lim et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13013), optional
reading — functions of the form
$f(v) + f(-v)$, extended to full basis invariance). RWSE's quiet
advantage — no sign to flip, no basis to rotate, twins provably identical
— is much of why it became the era's default diet; the widget above shows
Week 12's wallflower twins agreeing to machine precision. The two
families are complements, not rivals — local fingerprint and global
address — and serious recipes (GPS included) happily feed both.

## Graphormer: three doors into a standard transformer

The 2021 result that ended "transformers don't work on graphs" deserves
its context, because the stakes were unusually legible. OGB's
large-scale challenge that year
([Hu et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09430)) was PCQM4M:
predict a quantum-chemical
property (the HOMO-LUMO gap) for **3.8 million molecules**, a proxy task
for replacing expensive density-functional-theory computation with
learned models — chemistry's compute bill as an ML benchmark, with
industrial teams competing in public.

Message-passing entries crowded
the leaderboard; Graphormer — a Microsoft Research team — took first
place with a *standard transformer* whose slogan deserves quoting
precisely: *keep the architecture standard; smuggle the graph in through
the inputs and the attention bias.* The win mattered beyond the trophy:
molecules are small (attention's $n^2$ is cheap), data was large
(transformers' appetite finally fed), and the field's null hypothesis —
that graph structure demands graph-shaped architectures — lost a fair
fight on the biggest stage available. Every recipe since is a footnote
to that afternoon, including the hybrid that closes this lecture.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w13-graphormer.html >}}

Door one, **centrality encoding**: each node's degree indexes a learned
embedding added to its features — "how important am I," Week 2's first
lesson as a lookup table (in-degree and out-degree get separate tables on
directed graphs, Week 10's direction discipline persisting).

Door two, the deep one, is the **spatial encoding**.

::: {#def-w13-bias .definition name="Attention bias (spatial encoding)"}
For every pair $(u, v)$, the shortest-path distance indexes a learned
scalar $b_{\phi(u,v)}$ *added to the attention logit before the
softmax* — not a feature, a **prior over who should listen to whom**,
shared across heads' content whims. Read it as structure entering the
model between the scoring and the softmax, the one place a pairwise
quantity can live.
:::

Written out, Graphormer's biased logit is

$$
\operatorname{logit}(u, v) \;=\; \frac{q_u^\top k_v}{\sqrt d}
\;+\; b_{\phi(u,v)} \;+\; b'_{\operatorname{edge}(u,v)},
$$ {#eq-w13-graphormer}

where — $q_u^\top k_v / \sqrt d$ is the ordinary content score of
@eq-w13-attn; $\phi(u,v)$ is the **shortest-path-distance bucket** of
the pair (an integer, not a feature map — a different $\phi$ from the
linear-attention one later, which we will call $\psi$);
$b_{\phi(u,v)}$ is the learned scalar that bucket indexes, one per
distance per head; and $b'_{\operatorname{edge}(u,v)}$ is door three's
edge-encoding bias, computed from the edge features along the
$u$–$v$ shortest path. The
table of $b$'s is tiny (one scalar per distance value per head) but its
reach is total: every pair's logit, every layer.

Door three, **edge encoding**:
features of the edges along the shortest path between $u$ and $v$ —
averaged against learned per-hop weights — enter as the second logit
bias $b'$ in @eq-w13-graphormer,
so a bond's type modulates how two atoms attend across it.

One more Graphormer device deserves its sentence because you met its
ancestor in Week 9: a **virtual node** ([VNode]) connected to every real
node — the transformer's rendition of the master-node rewiring that
treated oversquashing, now doubling as a whole-graph readout token, the
[CLS] of molecules (the summary token BERT-style language models
prepend to every sequence). When you meet "global token" tricks anywhere in this
literature, this is the lineage.

Sit with the spatial bias until it reorganizes the week for you, and then
drive it yourself:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w13-bias.html >}}

If the learned $b$ decays with distance, attention concentrates on
neighbors — the model has *rediscovered message passing* as a soft
preference. If $b$ is flat, the graph dissolves. If it rises, the model
attends far-first — an anti-oversquashing specialist no MPNN can imitate.
Message passing is no longer a rival architecture; it is **one point in
the transformer's hypothesis space**, reachable by one bias profile among
many. That reframing — locality as a learnable prior rather than an
architectural law — is the deepest sentence of the week, and the exam will
ask for it.

## GraphGPS: the recipe, and our measured verdict

Graphormer's biases need all-pairs shortest paths — $O(n^2)$ memory before
training starts — and pure attention still scales quadratically. The
pragmatic synthesis, GraphGPS
([Rampášek et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12454) — required
reading, literally titled a
*recipe*), runs in every layer **two channels in parallel**: a local MPNN
over the real edges (structure, exactly, cheaply) and a global attention
over all nodes (range, when needed), summed and normalized, with PE/SE
features (RWSE, LapPE) feeding both. Modular by construction: swap the
MPNN flavor, swap the attention flavor (including linear-time
approximations when $n$ grows), choose your encodings per task.

Write the block down once, because Lab 13 makes you build it and the
equations are the specification: per layer,

$$X_{\text{loc}} = \mathrm{MPNN}(X, E), \qquad
X_{\text{glob}} = \mathrm{Attn}(X), \qquad
X' = \mathrm{LN}\big(X + X_{\text{loc}} + X_{\text{glob}}\big), \qquad
X'' = \mathrm{LN}\big(X' + \mathrm{FFN}(X')\big),$$ {#eq-w13-gps}

where — $X$ is the node-feature matrix (one row per node, with the
PE/SE vectors linearly mapped into it once at the input); $E$ is the
edge set with its features, read only by the local channel;
$\mathrm{LN}$ is LayerNorm; $\mathrm{FFN}$ is the transformer's
two-layer feed-forward block; and $X'$, $X''$ are the layer's
intermediate and final outputs.

As pseudocode — and this is exactly Lab 13's `Block` plus the
`global_channel` you write inside it — one layer runs:

::: {#alg-w13-gps .algorithm name="One GraphGPS Layer"}
Runs the local and global channels in parallel on a batch of graphs and
sums them into a shared residual stream.

**Input:** node features $X$ (encodings already summed in at the
input); edges $E$ with features; batch assignment of nodes to graphs.
**Output:** updated node features $X''$.

1. $X_{\text{loc}} \leftarrow \mathrm{MPNN}(X, E)$  (e.g. GINE — reads edge features)
2. $(\tilde X, \text{mask}) \leftarrow \operatorname{to\_dense\_batch}(X)$  (pad graphs to the batch max)
3. $X_{\text{glob}} \leftarrow \mathrm{MHA}(\tilde X, \tilde X, \tilde X;\ \text{key\_padding\_mask} = \lnot\text{mask})$
4. $X_{\text{glob}} \leftarrow X_{\text{glob}}[\text{mask}]$  (drop the padding rows)
5. $X' \leftarrow \mathrm{LN}(X + X_{\text{loc}} + X_{\text{glob}})$  (shared residual stream)
6. $X'' \leftarrow \mathrm{LN}(X' + \mathrm{FFN}(X'))$
7. **return** $X''$
:::

Step 3 hides the genre's quietest bug: `to_dense_batch` returns a mask
with True on *real* nodes, while `key_padding_mask` wants True on
*padding* — forget the inversion and attention reads phantom atoms,
which is precisely the sabotage Lab 13's assert prices. Cost per layer:
$O(Ed)$ for the local channel, $O(n^2 d)$ for the global one — the
bill the next paragraphs make concrete.

Note
what is deliberately boring in @eq-w13-gps: residuals everywhere (Week
7's repair shop,
standard-issue), LayerNorm rather than BatchNorm (Week 11's batch-
statistics pitfall, pre-solved), and *sum* as the channel combiner — the
two channels are colleagues writing to a shared workspace, not rivals to
arbitrate. The modularity is the point: the MPNN slot takes any Week 6–10
convolution; the attention slot takes full softmax attention at small $n$
or a linear-time approximation (kernel tricks that compute
attention-shaped aggregation in $O(n)$ — accepting approximation where
Week 11 accepted sampling variance, the same negotiation one level up)
when $n$ grows; the encoding slot takes whatever your task's structure
demands. A recipe, exactly as titled.

The engineering reality of the attention slot deserves its own honest
paragraph before any table, because $O(n^2)$ is a phrase until it is a
number. Full attention materializes an $n \times n$ score matrix per head
per layer: at $n = 23$ (a ZINC molecule) that is 529 scores — invisible;
at $n = 10{,}000$, one hundred million scores per head-layer — about
400 MB in float32, times heads, times layers, before gradients (Week
11's audit, squared as promised); at arxiv's $n = 169{,}343$, the score
matrix alone is 114 GB. Batching pads every graph to the batch's largest
member (our implementation's `to_dense_batch`), so one big molecule taxes
the whole batch. This is why "graph transformer" and "web-scale graph"
appear in the same sentence only alongside linear attention, sampling, or
a hybrid whose global channel is rationed — and why the *decision* this
section ends with has a cost column, not just an accuracy one.

Since the linear-attention escape hatch carries the whole "graph
transformers at scale" story, see how the trick actually works — it is
one associativity move. The expensive object in
$\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top)V$ (with $Q$, $K$, $V$ the stacked query,
key, and value matrices) is the $n \times n$ score matrix, forced
into existence because the softmax couples each row's entries. Suppose
instead the attention weight factorized as $\psi(q_v)^\top \psi(k_u)$
for some feature map $\psi$ (a new symbol on purpose — Graphormer's
$\phi$ was a distance bucket; this $\psi$ maps vectors to vectors):
then node $v$'s output regroups as

$$
\sum_u \psi(q_v)^\top \psi(k_u)\, \mathbf v_u^{\phantom\top}
\;=\;
\psi(q_v)^\top \Big(\sum_u \psi(k_u)\, \mathbf v_u^\top\Big),
$$ {#eq-w13-linear}

where — $q_v$, $k_u$, $\mathbf v_u$ are the query, key, and value
vectors of @eq-w13-attn; $\psi$ is the kernel feature map replacing the
softmax's coupling; and the
bracketed sum is one $d \times d$ matrix, computed once for the whole
graph in $O(n)$ and reused by every query. Reordering the parentheses
deletes the quadratic term. The catch: no finite $\psi$ reproduces the
softmax kernel exactly, so linear attentions (the Performer family —
[Choromanski et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.14794))
approximate it with randomized features, trading exactness for
tractability — precisely the negotiation Week 11 ran with sampling, one
level up the stack. When a paper says "our transformer scales to
million-node graphs," this bracket, or a sparsity pattern doing the same
job, is what it means.

Implementation notes from building exactly this — the details that cost
an afternoon each when unshared. ZINC's atoms arrive as integer types
(28 of them) and bonds as integers (4): both become learned embedding
tables, the atom embedding summed with the linearly-mapped RWSE vector
at the input — *summed, not concatenated*, so the encoding lives in the
same space the attention reasons in.

Batching many small graphs for the
attention channel requires densification: `to_dense_batch` pads every
graph to the batch's largest and returns the mask that must reach
attention as `key_padding_mask` — forget the mask and your model attends
to phantom atoms, a bug whose only symptom is mediocrity (Lab 13's
asserts check mask-invariance directly: adding a padded node must not
change any real node's output). And the local channel needs edge
features (`GINEConv`), or bond types silently vanish from the model that
was supposedly reading molecules. None of this is in the papers;
all of it is in the difference between reproducing a number and almost
reproducing it.

We built the budget version and ran the honest ladder — same data, same
100-epoch budget, same seed protocol:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w13-results.html >}}

{{< include ../assets/d3/w13-results.html >}}

First, the protocol card, because a table without one is an anecdote:
ZINC-subset (10,000 train / 1,000 val / 1,000 test molecules, the
community's standard 12k slice, protocol per
[Dwivedi et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.00982)),
constrained-solubility regression graded
by mean absolute error; every model 4 blocks of hidden width 64 with the
same GINE-style local convolution reading bond types; 100 epochs of Adam
at $10^{-3}$ under one cosine schedule (the learning rate glides
smoothly to zero along a cosine curve — deep-learning folklore, named
here once); test MAE reported at the best
validation epoch; one seed protocol shared by all rows. What we
deliberately did *not* do: per-model tuning, warmup schedules (a brief
low-learning-rate ramp at the start of training), larger
budgets — the comparison isolates *ingredients at matched cost*, which is
the question a working team actually faces on a Tuesday.

Read the result with Week 7's eyes. The **encoding paid**: 0.349 → 0.296,
six seconds of precompute, no architecture change — consistent with
everything Week 9 taught about what molecular tasks need (rings!) and
what MPNNs can't see about themselves. The **attention did not pay
here**: 0.303 at 2.7× the wall-clock, and the diagnosis is not
"attention is bad" but a sentence you can now write yourself: *ZINC
molecules average 23 atoms with single-digit diameters, so four local
layers already reach every atom — range was never the binding
constraint, and buying more of it bought nothing.*

One measured surprise
deserves its own sentence: the naive expectation "GPS ⊇ MPNN+RWSE, so
GPS ≥ MPNN+RWSE" is *false at fixed budget* — the attention channel's
extra parameters and slower steps are not free, and a superset
hypothesis class with the same optimizer time can land lower. (Week 9
said expressiveness is not a leaderboard; here even *capacity* isn't.)
Meanwhile the tuned literature reaches ≈0.070 with ~10× schedules,
warmups, and architecture polish — a number our table neither
contradicts nor reproduces, because *budget moves everything* and
comparing across budgets is the leaderboard sin this course has spent a
semester prosecuting. Both rows of truth fit in one honest paragraph;
most blog posts pick one.

When *does* the hybrid win decisively? Exactly where the diagnosis
predicts, and the field built a benchmark suite to prove it: the
long-range graph benchmarks
([Dwivedi et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08164)) assemble
tasks where the label provably
couples distant nodes — peptides whose properties depend on residues far
apart in the chain, image-derived graphs with global layout, code graphs
pairing definitions with distant uses — and on those leaderboards the
global channel's premium finally purchases accuracy that no depth of
local layers recovers (Week 9's sensitivity collapse said why: the
signal cannot squeeze through). GPS-style hybrids and their descendants
own those tables; plain MPNNs trail by margins no tuning closes. The
suite's existence is itself a methodological lesson worth copying: when
a community suspects an architecture's advantage is regime-specific,
the honest move is to *construct the regime* and measure — precisely
what our 23-atom molecules could not do for attention.

So the decision procedure is Week 11's constraint-first reading with one
new column: **estimate the task's required range against the graph's
diameter and bottlenecks** (the $(\hat A^K)_{uv}$ probe from Week 9 is
the instrument, and it costs one matrix power). Range needed and
structure needed → GPS-style hybrid. Structure only → MPNN + RWSE, the
quiet winner of our table and the option that also survives Week 11's
scale bills. Range only, enormous $n$ → linear attention or sampling,
and every Week 11 bill applies, squared. And in all three branches, the
encodings ride along near-free — the one ingredient with no failure
regime on this menu.

Run the procedure once on graphs you have already touched, as a
calibration. ZINC molecules: diameter single-digit, four layers cover
it — the range column is empty, buy encodings, which is our table's
verdict derived rather than observed. The arxiv citation graph:
$n = 169{,}343$ kills dense attention outright (that 114 GB score
matrix), so the menu is MPNN+RWSE or a linear-attention hybrid, and
Week 11's sampling bills decide between them. A blockchain-fraud graph
whose labels depend on funds hopping through long mule chains: range is
the *task*, locality is the failure — this is the hybrid's home turf,
and the one branch where paying attention's premium is not optional.
Three graphs, three different winners, one procedure — which is what
"architecture choice" should feel like by Week 13.

## What this does to Week 9's ceiling

A theory checkpoint, because the marketing in this genre routinely
garbles it. Does attention *itself* exceed the 1-WL ceiling? **No** — and
you can prove it with Week 9's own tools: on uniform features with no
encodings, every node of a regular graph presents identical queries,
keys, and values, attention weights come out uniform, and the update
reduces to mean-pooling everyone — *below* GIN, blind to everything WL is
blind to and more.

What exceeds the ceiling is the **encodings**: RWSE
carries cycle counts, LapPE carries spectral coordinates, spatial biases
carry distances — each a quantity provably outside message passing's
reach, injected as input. That is Week 9's Route 2 (structural features),
industrialized; the transformer is the *vehicle* that spends the extra
information well at range, not the source of it. Hence the honest slogan
for the whole genre, worth memorizing for the exam: **attention buys
range; encodings buy expressiveness; neither buys the other.** Our
measured table is that slogan wearing numbers — the encoding moved the
MAE, the attention moved the wall-clock.

The checkpoint deserves its formal statement, because it is the week's
most-garbled claim in the wild.

::: {.proposition #prp-w13-attn-wl}
Pure self-attention with no positional or structural input computes a
function of the *multiset of node features only*. Consequently any two
graphs with the same feature multiset — regardless of their edges —
receive identical outputs, and the model is strictly weaker than 1-WL:
it cannot even separate the 4-node path from the 4-node star on uniform
features, which 1-WL distinguishes in one round.
:::

The proof is the mean-pooling fact from this lecture's first section,
run by induction. With identical features, every node emits the same
query, key, and value; all logits tie; every softmax row is uniform;
every node receives the same mean and applies the same update — so
representations stay identical layer after layer, and nothing
edge-dependent ever enters (the edge set appears nowhere in the
computation). 1-WL, by contrast, reads degrees off the graph in its
first refinement — the path's multiset $\{1,1,2,2\}$ against the
star's $\{1,1,1,3\}$ — and separates immediately. Attention without a
positional diet is not "expressive but expensive"; it is blind *and*
expensive, and every impressive graph-transformer number in the
literature is therefore a claim about its encodings.

And a forward pointer that explains the field's current excitement:
because a transformer's input is "a set of feature vectors plus biases,"
it is *format-agnostic* in a way message passing never was — the same
architecture ingests molecules, KGs (Week 10's ULTRA runs on this
insight), text-attributed graphs, and mixtures, which is precisely the
substrate a *foundation model* needs. The graph-transformer literature
of this week is, among other things, the plumbing being laid for
pretrained graph models; when they arrive in force, their positional
diets will be the encodings you hand-computed today.

## The method: positioning a new "graph transformer" paper in five questions

The genre is prolific; the questions that sort it are stable.

1. **Where does the graph enter** — features, attention bias, masking,
   or auxiliary loss? (Everything else is marketing; this is the
   architecture.)
2. **What does attention cost** — full $O(n^2)$, sparse, or linear
   approximation — and at the paper's own benchmark sizes, does that
   matter?
3. **Which encodings carry the load** — and does the ablation table
   separate their contribution from attention's? (Ours did; many
   don't — and RWSE-vs-attention is exactly the confound to check.)
4. **What is the MPNN baseline** — tuned with the same budget, with the
   same encodings? (An MPNN+RWSE baseline beats naive transformers on
   many published tables once someone bothers to run it.)
5. **Does the win survive the budget column?** Same epochs, same tuning
   effort, or the comparison is a schedule masquerading as an
   architecture.

Five questions, and you can locate any paper in this literature in ten
minutes — including the ones not yet written.

Watch the questions run on a composite of the genre — call it
*GraphMegaFormer*, claiming "+2.1 over GCN on four benchmarks." Where
does the graph enter? Appendix C reveals: RWSE plus a distance bias —
so the architecture is GPS-shaped, whatever the branding. Attention
cost? Full $O(n^2)$; the largest benchmark graph has 500 nodes — fine
there, silent about scale. Which encodings carry the load? The ablation
removes attention (−0.3) but never removes RWSE — the biggest
ingredient is uncredited, and our table says it may be most of the 2.1.
The baseline? GCN *without* encodings, on 2019 hyperparameters. Budget?
Their model gets 400 epochs with warmup; the GCN gets 100 flat.

Verdict
in ten minutes: a probably-fine architecture wrapped in a comparison
that overstates it — read the idea, re-run the table yourself. That
skill, exercised on a paper that does not exist, is the actual
deliverable of this section.

For the map's completeness, three named landmarks you will meet when
the questions run on real papers, each slotting instantly once you ask
*where does the graph enter*. SAN
([Kreuzer et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03893)) feeds
*learned functions of the
Laplacian spectrum* as positions — LapPE with the sign problem attacked
by architecture — and pays full quadratic attention. TokenGT
([Kim et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02505)) goes
radical: edges become *tokens* alongside nodes, the graph serialized
into a longer sequence for an utterly standard transformer — maximal
standardization, maximal sequence length, the bet being that
transformer infrastructure improves faster than graph-specific code
(a bet the LLM era keeps paying out).

Exphormer
([Shirzad et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06147)) answers the
cost
question instead: attention restricted to the real edges *plus* a
random expander overlay — Week 9's rewiring vocabulary returning as a
sparsity pattern, global mixing at $O(n)$ edges without global cost.
Three papers, three doors, no new questions needed — the five you have
already sort them, which is the point of owning questions rather than
paper lists.

One synthesis before the pitfalls, reading this week's widget quartet as
a single argument. The reach-vs-cost toggle showed the bare trade —
range for $n^2$ — and its molecule-sized loophole (144 pair scores is
nothing). The RWSE fingerprints showed the graph re-entering as numbers
with meanings — twins identical to machine precision, hubs and leaves
separated by a vector you can audit entry by entry.

The bias explorer
showed the deepest reframe: locality as one *setting* of a learned dial,
message passing demoted from law to prior. And the measured ladder
showed the market clearing: at honest prices, the encoding sold and the
attention sat on the shelf — for this task, at this size, at this
budget. Four interactives, one thesis: *the graph transformer is not a
new species; it is the old toolbox, re-plumbed through attention, and
every purchasing decision in it is one this course has already taught
you to price.*

A caution that spans both encoding families before the list: encodings
are *statistics of the training distribution's graphs*, and they shift
when the graphs do. A model trained on 20-atom molecules meets a
40-atom molecule at test time: its RWSE entries land in ranges the
linear map never saw, its LapPE coordinates live on different spectra —
and degradation arrives without any error message. Size
extrapolation is a known soft spot of the whole genre; if your
deployment's graphs grow, your validation set should grow first.

## Common pitfalls

**Feeding attention a graph with no positional diet.** Pure attention on
raw node features is a set model: two different molecules with equal atom
multisets are *provably identical* to it — below even the 1-WL ceiling.
The encodings are not a garnish; they are the graph — and the symptom
is sneaky, because the model still trains and still scores above chance
on feature-heavy tasks, so nothing crashes while structure silently
contributes zero.

**Comparing a transformer-with-RWSE against an MPNN-without.** The most
common confound in the genre, and our table shows why it matters: RWSE
alone was worth 0.053 MAE — likely more than many published
architecture margins. Give both sides the same diet before crediting the
attention; when a paper doesn't, you can often reconstruct the honest
comparison from its own ablation appendix.

**LapPE without sign handling.** Train with one eigenvector sign, test
with the flip — silent degradation that reproduces nowhere and varies
across library versions (eigensolvers make different arbitrary choices).
Randomize, absolutize, or use invariant nets; never ignore.

**Forgetting the padding mask.** Batched dense attention over
variable-size graphs attends to padding unless told not to; the model
still trains, merely worse, and the bug survives every test that does
not explicitly check invariance to added padding. Lab 13's assert does;
copy it into your own code forever.

**All-pairs precomputes at scale.** Graphormer's spatial table is
$O(n^2)$ *storage*; on Week 11's graphs that is the whole GPU before a
single parameter loads. Hybrids and linear attentions exist precisely for
this; check the paper's largest graph before importing its architecture.

**Treating our 0.303 as "attention doesn't work."** It is one budget, one
scale, one task family — the same table at 10× budget or on long-range
tasks reverses. The transferable claim is the *diagnosis method*, not
the row ordering; quoting the row without the regime is exactly the sin
Figure 4's budget-reference toggle exists to inoculate against.

## In this week's lab

[Lab 13](../labs/lab13.qmd): you implement RWSE from the definition and
hit the hand-computed numbers exactly — including the tail node's zero,
asserted to four decimals, because a structural encoding you cannot
verify by hand is a bug you cannot see; you re-crack Week 9's CSL pair
with your own encoding (the two vertex-transitive graphs separate at
$k{=}3$, on your numbers) and separate triangle-members from tail nodes
with nothing but a threshold; you train the MPNN baseline on real ZINC
molecules and then assemble the GPS block yourself — parallel local and
global channels, LayerNorms, and the padding mask whose absence is the
genre's quietest bug (the assert adds a phantom node and demands your
real outputs not move). The lecture's 100-epoch table is provided for
your claims paragraph, which must include the honest sentence about what
attention did not buy; the stretch reruns the ladder at your own budget
and lets you watch the ordering breathe.

## Required reading

- **[Ying et al., 2021 — Do Transformers Really Perform Bad for Graph
  Representation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05234)** (NeurIPS 2021).
  Graphormer. §3.1's three encodings are
  the paper; the OGB-LSC result is the receipt. Read the spatial-encoding
  paragraph twice — it is the week's central idea.
- **[Rampášek et al., 2022 — Recipe for a General, Powerful, Scalable
  Graph Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12454)** (NeurIPS 2022).
  GraphGPS. Read §2 for the parallel-block
  design and Table 4 for the ablation discipline — encodings and attention
  credited separately, the honesty our own table imitates.

Optional: [Dwivedi & Bresson, 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.09699)
for the first serious generalization
and its LapPE lineage — read it as history: written *before* the field
knew which encodings would win, it frames the questions our five-question
method answers. [SignNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13013) (Lim et
al., ICLR 2023) for sign/basis invariance done
properly — go here if the LapPE ambiguity paragraph left you wanting the
construction rather than the workaround.
[Müller et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04181) (TMLR) —
*Attending to Graph Transformers* — the survey to consult before
believing any claim in this genre, including ours: its taxonomy is our
"where does the graph enter" question run over the whole literature,
and its experiments confirm the encoding-vs-attention confound at scale.
Reading order if you read only one: Graphormer's §3.1, then our Figure 4
again — the pair is the week.

## Check your understanding

**Q1.** Compute, by hand, the $k=2$ and $k=3$ RWSE entries for the tail
node (3) of the triangle-with-tail, and state what the $k=3$ value
detects.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
$k{=}2$: the tail's only move is to the hub (prob 1), which returns with
prob $\tfrac13$: $1 \cdot \tfrac13 = 0.333$. $k{=}3$: a return in three
steps requires a 3-cycle through node 3; there is none, so **exactly 0**.
The $k{=}3$ diagonal of $M^3$ counts (degree-weighted) triangles at the
node — the quantity Week 9 proved message passing cannot compute, now an
input feature.
</details>

**Q2.** Why is pure attention on raw features *weaker* than the 1-WL
ceiling, not stronger?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Without positional/structural input, attention never reads the edge set at
all: it processes the node feature *multiset*. Two non-isomorphic graphs
with identical feature multisets (any two graphs on the same uniform
features!) are indistinguishable — a failure even degree-aware 1-WL
avoids at round one. Range without structure is a downgrade; the
encodings restore structure and only then does the range advantage exist.
</details>

**Q3.** Where exactly does Graphormer's spatial encoding enter the
attention computation, and why is "bias" rather than "feature" the right
word?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
As a learned scalar $b_{\phi(u,v)}$ added to the pre-softmax logit
$\frac{q_u \cdot k_v}{\sqrt d} + b_{\phi(u,v)}$ — pair-indexed, not
node-indexed, so it cannot be absorbed into any node's features. It acts
as a prior over the attention distribution itself: content can override
it, but the default listening pattern is distance-shaped — which is why a
decaying $b$ reproduces message passing as a special case.
</details>

**Q4.** Your colleague's new graph transformer beats their MPNN baseline
by 0.04 MAE. Applying this lecture's method, name the two first questions
you ask about the comparison.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Did the MPNN baseline get the same positional/structural encodings? (Ours
gained 0.053 from RWSE alone — more than their whole margin.) And were
budgets matched — epochs, schedule, tuning effort? If either answer is
no, the table measures the confound, not the architecture. (Then: what
does attention cost at their $n$, and does the win survive on a
long-range task where it should be largest?)
</details>

**Q5.** A 500k-node fraud graph, task requires 6-hop context through known
bottlenecks. Assess: pure Graphormer, GPS-hybrid, MPNN+RWSE.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Pure Graphormer: the all-pairs spatial table alone is $2.5 \times 10^{11}$
entries — dead on arrival (Week 11's audit). MPNN+RWSE: cheap, but 6 hops
through bottlenecks is Week 9's squashing regime — the exact failure the
task description advertises. GPS-hybrid with *linear* global attention:
the design center — local channel for structure, linear attention for
range at $O(n)$, RWSE for both; budget the memory with Week 11's bill
before committing.
</details>

**Q6.** State the sign-ambiguity problem in one sentence and rank the
three standard treatments by information preserved.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
An eigenvector $v$ and $-v$ are equally valid, so LapPE hands the model
coordinates whose signs are arbitrary per graph and per run. Most
preserving: sign/basis-invariant networks (SignNet — learns functions
invariant by construction); middle: sign randomization in training
(model must learn the invariance, costs capacity); least: absolute
values (invariant but collapses $v$ and $|v|$ distinctions —
genuinely different positions merge).
</details>

**Q7.** Our GPS-lite lost to MPNN+RWSE at 100 epochs, yet GPS leads
long-range benchmarks. Reconcile in two sentences using this course's
vocabulary.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
ZINC's 23-atom molecules have diameters a 4-layer MPNN covers, so
attention's only unique product — range — had no buyer, while its extra
parameters and slower steps cost real budget (an ablation-shaped fact,
not an architecture verdict). Long-range benchmarks are built so that
bottlenecked, distant signal decides the task — Week 9's sensitivity
collapse territory — where the global channel is the *only* channel that
delivers, and the hybrid's premium finally purchases something.
</details>

**Q8.** Design the two-line experiment that decides whether a task needs
the global channel *before* training any transformer.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Week 9's probe: compute $(\hat A^K)_{uv}$ sensitivities between
task-relevant node pairs at feasible $K$ (plus the graph's diameter
distribution). If relevant pairs sit at tiny sensitivity or beyond
reachable depth, range binds → global channel justified; if
neighborhoods already cover the signal, spend the budget on encodings —
our table's exact verdict, predicted for free.
</details>

::: {.notions}
**Notions introduced this week**

- **Self-attention (query / key / value)** — a soft dictionary lookup:
  learned projections score every pair, softmax weights average the
  values (@def-w13-attention, @eq-w13-attn).
- **Random-walk structural encoding (RWSE)** — the vector of $k$-step
  return probabilities, a hand-checkable structure detector
  (@def-w13-rwse, @alg-w13-rwse).
- **Laplacian positional encoding (LapPE)** — coordinates in the
  Laplacian's low-frequency eigenbasis, defined only up to sign
  (@def-w13-lappe).
- **Attention bias (spatial encoding)** — a learned per-distance scalar
  added to the logit: locality as a prior, not a law (@def-w13-bias,
  @eq-w13-graphormer).
- **Virtual node** — a global token wired to every real node; Week 9's
  master-node rewiring as a transformer readout.
- **GraphGPS block** — parallel local MPNN and global attention summed
  into one residual stream (@eq-w13-gps, @alg-w13-gps).
- **Linear attention** — the kernel-factorized regrouping that deletes
  the $n^2$ score matrix (@eq-w13-linear).
- **Padding mask** — the flag telling batched dense attention which
  rows are phantom; forgetting it is the genre's quietest bug.
:::

## Where this leaves us

The wall between "GNNs" and "transformers" came down and revealed a dial:
locality as a learnable prior, with message passing at one end, pure
attention at the other, and the honest answer — measured on our own table
— task- and budget-dependent. The graph, evicted from the architecture,
re-entered as features you have been computing since Week 2; the sole
genuinely new object this week was the *attention bias*, and even that is
a distance table wearing a learned coat.

Notice also what kind of week this was, because the shape recurs in
every maturing subfield. No new theory arrived: the ceiling is still
Week 9's, the costs are still Week 11's, the splits are still Week 12's.
What arrived was a *recombination* — old quantities (returns,
eigenvectors, distances) meeting an old architecture (attention) under
an old discipline (matched-budget measurement) — and recombinations are
where most working progress in mature fields actually lives. The
student who memorized architectures has to start over this week; the
student who owns the quantities just watched them get re-plumbed. That
asymmetry is the course's whole bet, and next week — the production
tour — is where it pays out in job descriptions rather than benchmarks.

Close the loop — one minute, no notes: the tail node's $k{=}3$ return and
what it detects; the three Graphormer doors; the two-channel GPS block;
and our ladder's verdict with its one-sentence diagnosis. Then rehearse
the five paper-sorting questions once — they are the part you will still
use when this week's architectures are historical footnotes.

One lecture of new machinery remains, and it is the one that pays the
bills. Next week: graphs in *production* — time entering the picture
(temporal graphs and TGN's memory), recommenders at planetary scale
(LightGCN, and the PinSage story completing), relational deep learning
(Week 10's bridge, driven across at last), and the map of where this
field actually employs people. Bring Week 11's cost instincts and Week
12's split discipline; production is where both stop being homework.
